design_detail: Prospective population-based twin cohort (Minnesota Twin Family Study; same-sex pairs born 1977–1984), assessed at target ages 11 (intake, n=1512), 14 (FU1, n=1404) and 24 (FU4, n=1328). Two self-reported early exposures by the age-14 assessment (FU1, mean age 14.8: any alcoholic drink without parental permission; ever intoxicated) were related to 12 adult outcomes at about 25 in two ways: inverse-probability weighting on a propensity score built from 29 intake covariates (GEE for twin clustering), and co-twin control, which estimates the within-pair effect in pairs discordant for the exposure (all pairs, then MZ and DZ separately).
can_establish: Whether drinking and intoxication by about 14 go with adult substance-related and social outcomes at about 25 after balancing 29 measured childhood characteristics, and after holding constant what co-twins share (rearing environment, and all or half of their genes), in a Minnesota twin cohort born 1977–1984.
cannot_establish: That early drinking causes the adult outcomes: within-pair differences can still reflect confounders that differ between co-twins (for example a twin's own experimentation with tobacco or other drugs before 14, or different peers) and exposure measurement error; the within-MZ-pair estimates, the cleanest test, were significant for only a few outcomes and rest on small numbers of discordant pairs; nothing about amount or frequency of early drinking (two binary exposures) or about mechanism.

sample.recruitment: Population-based longitudinal study of twins born in Minnesota and their families (called community-based in the abstract); this analysis uses same-sex pairs from the cohort born 1977–1984, first assessed at a target age of 11 and followed every three or four years (Methods › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Same-sex twin pairs of the 1977–1984 birth cohort; other criteria are in earlier MTFS reports and not restated here.
sample.demographics: Intake: mean age 11.72 (SD 0.43), 50.3% female; FU1: 14.8 (0.53), 50.6% female; FU4: 25.29 (0.74), 51.4% female; 64% MZ and 36% DZ twins (Methods › Participants). Ethnicity and socioeconomic status entered the propensity model (Tables 1A and 1B) but their distributions are not reported in the main text.
sample.attrition: 1404 of 1512 (92.9%) assessed at 14 and 1328 (87.8%) at 24 (editors' arithmetic). How missing outcome data were handled, and whether those lost differed from those retained, is not reported in the main text; 'additional statistical and data-related considerations' are in the supplement, which was not read.
sample.selection_effects: A population-based twin sample from one US state, with 12% loss by 24. The co-twin analyses use only pairs discordant for the exposure: 20% of MZ and 26% of DZ pairs for early use, and 9% and 12% for early intoxication. If those percentages apply to all 486 MZ and 270 DZ pairs, about 97 MZ and 70 DZ pairs were discordant for early use and about 44 MZ and 32 DZ pairs for early intoxication (editors' arithmetic; the paper gives no pair counts).

exposure.measurement: Self-report at the age-14 assessment, recorded at the time rather than recalled in adulthood: ever having had an alcoholic drink without parental permission by FU1 (505 exposed) and ever having been intoxicated by FU1 (212 exposed). Rates were similar by zygosity (χ2(1)=0.192, p=0.66; χ2(1)=0.691, p=0.41) and are said to approximate national rates for adolescents of the same cohort and age (Methods › Measures › Early Adolescent Alcohol Exposure Measures at Target Age 14).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured: both exposures are binary, with no amount, frequency or age within the window; drinking with parental permission counts as unexposed.
exposure.polysubstance: The twin's own tobacco or other drug use before 14 is not among the 29 propensity covariates, which are all measured at 11 and include parental alcohol, tobacco and drug use (Tables 1A and 1B); adult tobacco, cannabis and other drug use are outcomes.

comparison.controls: Propensity-score analyses: twins without the early exposure, weighted by 1/(1-PS), against exposed twins weighted by 1/PS. Co-twin control: the unexposed co-twin in exposure-discordant pairs, through the within-pair (individual-level) coefficient (Methods › Statistical Analyses).
comparison.matching: Weighting on 29 intake covariates (9 individual-level, such as IQ, puberty, school performance, externalizing symptoms and delinquency; 20 family-level, such as sex, age, ethnicity, parental education, income, psychopathology and substance use) reduced the mean absolute standardized difference from 0.23 to 0.03 for early use and from 0.29 to 0.07 for early intoxication, all below the 0.25 threshold used. Within discordant pairs, individual-level covariates were balanced except puberty in DZ pairs discordant for intoxication (0.31) (Results › Propensity Score and Inverse Probability of Treatment Weights; Tables 1A and 1B).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Factors that differ between co-twins and precede the exposure but were not measured (own early tobacco or drug use, peer group, traits beyond the measured externalizing, school and family variables); in DZ pairs half of the genetic variation; prenatal and perinatal differences.

outcomes.instruments: Twelve outcomes at FU4, described only in the supplement (not read): alcohol use quantity and frequency index; alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms; tobacco use quantity and frequency index; number of times used marijuana; number of drug classes ever used; drug abuse or dependence symptoms; adult antisocial behavior symptoms; dependent stressful life events; family relationships; interpersonal problems; social engagement; adult independence (Tables 2A and 2B).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not described in the main text.
outcomes.operationalization: Standardized regression coefficients (β) for each binary exposure on each outcome; the scaling of the 'standardized estimates' is not explained in the main text. Alcohol 'problems' are symptom counts of abuse or dependence, not diagnoses.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 12 outcomes × 2 exposures × 5 analyses (unweighted, weighted, co-twin all pairs, MZ, DZ) give 120 coefficients judged at p<0.05, plus zygosity moderation tests.

analysis.effect_sizes: Tables 2A and 2B, β (SE) as printed. Early alcohol use: alcohol use index, unweighted 0.63 (0.06), propensity-weighted 0.57 (0.06), co-twin all pairs 0.21 (0.09), MZ 0.22 (0.10), DZ 0.20 (0.14); alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms 0.46, 0.36, 0.24 (0.11), MZ 0.17 (0.14), DZ 0.34 (0.16); tobacco index 0.63, 0.49, 0.21 (0.09), MZ 0.09, DZ 0.39; times used marijuana 0.54, 0.43, 0.28 (0.10), MZ 0.22 (0.11), DZ 0.38; drug classes 0.73, 0.60, 0.44 (0.10), MZ 0.41 (0.12), DZ 0.50 (0.17); drug abuse or dependence symptoms 0.51, 0.40, 0.27 (0.11), MZ 0.18, DZ 0.42; antisocial symptoms 0.52, 0.38, 0.19 (0.09), MZ 0.08, DZ 0.37; dependent stressful life events 0.35, 0.26, 0.26 (0.10), MZ 0.26 (0.11), DZ 0.26. Early intoxication: alcohol use index 0.62, 0.57, 0.37 (0.13), MZ 0.26 (0.17), DZ 0.54 (0.23); alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms 0.53, 0.31, 0.29 (0.15), MZ 0.15, DZ 0.51; tobacco 0.68, 0.50, 0.25 (0.12), MZ 0.16, DZ 0.38; marijuana 0.60, 0.31, 0.43 (0.17), MZ 0.27, DZ 0.66; drug classes 0.84, 0.62, 0.50 (0.16), MZ 0.38 (0.15), DZ 0.68; drug abuse or dependence symptoms 0.68, 0.38, 0.47 (0.16), MZ 0.26, DZ 0.78; antisocial 0.60, 0.43, 0.18 (0.16), MZ 0.08, DZ 0.35; dependent stressful life events 0.47, 0.40, 0.38 (0.15), MZ 0.43 (0.18), DZ 0.30. Family relationships, interpersonal problems, social engagement and adult independence were not associated with either exposure after weighting or within pairs. Zygosity did not significantly moderate any within-pair effect. Significance in this card is taken from β and SE, not from the printed p-values (see reporting issues).
analysis.covariates: Propensity score from 29 intake covariates (Tables 1A and 1B; full list and descriptions in supplementary Table S1, not read); co-twin control removes factors shared within pairs.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 12 outcomes are reported for every analysis in Tables 2A and 2B. The text's summaries of those tables are partly inaccurate (see reporting issues), and outcome definitions and data handling are only in the supplement.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Co-twin estimates rest on roughly 97 MZ and 70 DZ discordant pairs for early use and 44 MZ and 32 DZ pairs for early intoxication (editors' estimate from the discordance percentages), so most MZ-only estimates are imprecise and their non-significance is not evidence of no effect.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Drinking and intoxication by 14 were associated with adult alcohol use, other substance use, antisocial symptoms and stressful life events of the person's own making, after propensity weighting and, attenuated, within discordant twin pairs; the unweighted associations with interpersonal problems and adult independence lost nominal significance after weighting (for adult independence through a larger standard error, the coefficient barely changing), and no social-functioning outcome was associated within pairs. Within MZ pairs, which control for all genes and the shared environment, the association reached significance for the alcohol-use index (early use), number of drug classes used and dependent stressful life events, was borderline for marijuana use (early use), and was not significant for alcohol or drug abuse and dependence symptoms, tobacco or antisocial symptoms.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that early alcohol exposures 'predict adult alcohol problems and related outcomes' despite stringent adjustment, and that propensity-score estimates were likely biased by unmeasured confounding; the Discussion says the analyses support a causal effect of early alcohol use on adult functioning. Gaps: (1) for alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms the within-pair association held only for early use across all discordant pairs (β 0.24), not within MZ pairs (0.17, SE 0.14) and not for early intoxication (0.29, SE 0.15); (2) 'adult functioning' overstates a result that was null for every social-functioning outcome; (3) the inference that propensity estimates were biased rests on within-pair estimates being smaller, which exposure measurement error can also produce (as the authors note), and which did not hold for early intoxication with marijuana use and drug abuse or dependence symptoms (larger within pairs than after weighting); (4) causal wording is used although non-shared confounding is not excluded. The final paragraph is more cautious, saying effects may be causal only in the absence of such confounding and that more research is needed.

timeline.event: Prescott & Kendler, twins: the association of age at first drink with alcoholism judged largely non-causal and attributed to common genetic effects (as cited in the introduction).
Grant J.D. et al., twin design: adolescent alcohol use a risk factor for adult alcohol and drug dependence, not wholly explained by familial factors (as cited).
Odgers et al., Dunedin cohort: after propensity-score matching, substance use before 15 kept associations with adult substance dependence and convictions (as cited).
Deutsch et al., Australian twins: age at first drink associated with adult alcohol involvement beyond shared familial factors, moderated by family context (as cited).
Maimaris & McCambridge, systematic review of prospective general-population cohorts (read in this round): sparse and mixed evidence, with no twin or sibling design among the five included reports.
This study (online October 2014): propensity weighting and co-twin control in the Minnesota Twin Family Study.

replication.where_it_stands: The study agrees with the earlier co-twin reports it cites (Grant et al., 2006; Deutsch et al., 2013) that associations of early drinking with adult alcohol and drug outcomes are reduced but not removed within twin pairs, against the earlier non-causal reading of Prescott & Kendler (1999). The within-MZ-pair results are mostly imprecise, and residual non-shared confounding is not excluded. The round's reading list names Richmond-Rakerd et al. (2016) as the other DOI-bearing twin test; it was not read here.

funding.funder: Not reported: the author manuscript on PMC carries no funding or acknowledgments statement (the published version was not read).
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors are at the Department of Psychology, University of Minnesota, which runs the Minnesota Twin Family Study; the second and third authors are authors of several of the cited earlier MTFS and twin-method papers (refs 5, 11, 17, 20, 21).

what_would_settle_it: Pooled analyses of MZ twin pairs discordant for early drinking across several twin registries, large enough to estimate within-MZ-pair effects on DSM alcohol and drug use disorders with precision, with early drinking measured repeatedly (age, amount, intoxication) and the twins' own behaviour and substance use before the exposure measured; together with natural experiments that shift the age of first drinking for reasons unrelated to the person.

domains.note: Propensity weighting balanced 29 measured childhood covariates, and the co-twin design removes everything shared within pairs (all genes in MZ pairs, half in DZ pairs); confounders that differ between co-twins, including the twin's own early tobacco or drug use, are not addressed.

Two binary self-reports at 14, recorded close to the time; drinking with parental permission counts as unexposed, and random misclassification, which the authors note, biases within-pair estimates toward zero.
Population-based twin cohort entered at 11, before the exposure.
No interventions relevant to the exposure–outcome relation are described.
12% of the intake sample was not assessed at 24; handling of missing data and the comparison of those lost with those retained are only in the supplement (not read).
Adult outcomes are self-reported symptom counts and indices, described only in the supplement; whether assessors knew the adolescent data is not reported.

All 120 coefficients are tabulated, which is good, but none are corrected for multiplicity, the printed p-values are wrong (see reporting issues) and the text's summary departs from the tables in places.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A strong design for this question: exposure measured at 14 in a population-based cohort, balanced on a rich set of childhood measures, and tested within twin pairs. The remaining threats are non-shared confounding, small numbers of MZ discordant pairs, attrition handled only in the supplement, and reporting errors in the p-values and in the text's summary of the tables. Cite it for the attenuated but persisting association of early drinking with adult alcohol use and with the number of drug classes used within twin pairs, including MZ pairs, and for the absence of associations with adult social functioning; not for a causal effect on alcohol use disorder, which within MZ pairs was not shown.

key_findings.finding: Minnesota Twin Family Study, same-sex pairs born 1977–1984: 1512 twins at 11 (50.3% female; 972 MZ, 540 DZ), 1404 at 14 and 1328 at about 25. By the age-14 assessment (FU1, mean age 14.8), 505 had drunk alcohol without parental permission and 212 had been intoxicated.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants; Methods › Measures › Early Adolescent Alcohol Exposure Measures at Target Age 14

key_findings.finding: Before weighting, 13 of 29 childhood covariates differed by a standardized difference of about 0.25 or more between twins who had drunk by 14 and those who had not (19 of 29 for intoxication), notably delinquent behaviours (0.51; 0.79) and parental tobacco and alcohol use; weighting reduced the mean absolute difference from 0.23 to 0.03 (use) and from 0.29 to 0.07 (intoxication).
key_findings.locator: Results › Propensity Score and Inverse Probability of Treatment Weights, 2nd paragraph; Tables 1A and 1B

key_findings.finding: After propensity weighting, early alcohol use remained associated with the adult alcohol-use index (β 0.57, SE 0.06), alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms (0.36), tobacco (0.49), marijuana (0.43), number of drug classes (0.60), drug abuse or dependence symptoms (0.40), antisocial symptoms (0.38) and dependent stressful life events (0.26). The unweighted associations with interpersonal problems and adult independence lost nominal significance after weighting, in different ways: for interpersonal problems the coefficient fell (0.15, SE 0.06, to 0.08, SE 0.08); for adult independence it barely changed (0.16, SE 0.07, to 0.15, SE 0.08) and the standard error grew (for early intoxication, 0.18 before and after weighting, Table 2B).
key_findings.locator: Results › Estimated Effects of Early Alcohol Exposures on Adult Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 2A; Table 2B (adult independence)

key_findings.finding: Within all exposure-discordant pairs, early alcohol use was associated with the alcohol-use index (β 0.21, SE 0.09), alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms (0.24, 0.11), tobacco (0.21, 0.09), marijuana (0.28, 0.10), drug classes (0.44, 0.10), drug abuse or dependence symptoms (0.27, 0.11), antisocial symptoms (0.19, 0.09) and dependent stressful life events (0.26, 0.10), all with β/SE of about 2 or more.
key_findings.locator: Table 2A, Cotwin control: All discordant pairs; Results › Estimated Effects…, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Within MZ pairs discordant for early use, associations with β/SE of about 2 or more were found for the alcohol-use index (0.22, SE 0.10), number of drug classes (0.41, 0.12) and dependent stressful life events (0.26, 0.11), with marijuana borderline (0.22, 0.11); alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms (0.17, 0.14), tobacco (0.09), drug abuse or dependence symptoms (0.18) and antisocial symptoms (0.08) were not significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 2A, Cotwin control: Discordant MZ pairs
key_findings.note: Judged from β and SE because the printed p-values are not valid (see reporting issues); the MZ estimates rest on roughly 97 discordant pairs (editors' estimate).

key_findings.finding: For early intoxication, within all discordant pairs: alcohol-use index 0.37 (SE 0.13), tobacco 0.25 (0.12), marijuana 0.43 (0.17), drug classes 0.50 (0.16), drug abuse or dependence symptoms 0.47 (0.16) and dependent stressful life events 0.38 (0.15) were associated; alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms (0.29, SE 0.15) and antisocial symptoms (0.18, 0.16) were not. Within MZ pairs only drug classes (0.38, 0.15) and stressful life events (0.43, 0.18) were.

Zygosity did not significantly moderate any within-pair effect, but several substance-related within-pair estimates were larger in DZ than in MZ pairs (for example drug abuse or dependence symptoms after intoxication, DZ 0.78 vs MZ 0.26), which the authors read as partial genetic confounding in DZ pairs.
key_findings.locator: Results › Estimated Effects…, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph; Tables 2A and 2B

key_findings.finding: Neither exposure was significantly associated with family relationships, interpersonal problems, social engagement or adult independence after weighting or within pairs. After weighting, the adult-independence estimates were not near zero but missed significance (early use 0.15, SE 0.08; early intoxication 0.18, SE 0.11); within pairs they were 0.00 and 0.01.
key_findings.locator: Tables 2A and 2B, lower four rows; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that the co-twin design cannot separate causal effects from confounders not shared by co-twins, and that random error in the exposure also shrinks within-pair estimates relative to unpaired ones.

reporting_issues.issue: The p-values in Tables 2A and 2B cannot be two-sided p-values from the coefficients and standard errors shown. Coefficients of zero or nearly zero carry p-values of about 0.39 to 0.40 (for example 0.00, SE 0.12, p=0.396; 0.01, SE 0.15, p=0.396; -0.02, SE 0.25, p=0.397), where a Wald test would give values near 1. Across the tables the printed values match the standard normal density at β/SE, which peaks at 0.399, rather than tail probabilities (editors' check: 0.09/0.12 gives density 0.30 and two-sided p 0.45, printed 0.291; 0.08/0.11 gives 0.31 and 0.47, printed 0.312; -0.06/0.10 gives 0.33 and 0.55, printed 0.332; 0.08/0.08 gives 0.242 and 0.32, printed 0.242). One printed value fits neither reading: MZ pairs, number of drug classes after early use, 0.41 (SE 0.12), printed p=0.004, where the density is about 0.001 and the two-sided p about 0.0006 (editors' check).
reporting_issues.consequence: No printed p-value should be quoted, including the abstract's p=0.031 for the co-twin alcohol-use estimate (two-sided p about 0.02 from 0.21 and 0.09, editors' calculation, imprecise because of rounding). Above |z| of about 1.6 the density is slightly larger than the true p, so the paper's significance calls are, if anything, slightly conservative: for example MZ marijuana after early use (0.22, SE 0.11, printed 0.055) has a two-sided p near 0.05.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that within-pair effects of both exposures were attenuated relative to the weighted estimates and remained significant for the alcohol and substance-use outcomes, with only antisocial behavior lost for intoxication. In Table 2B, early intoxication's within-pair association with alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms was not significant (0.29, SE 0.15, printed p=0.061), and its within-pair estimates for marijuana (0.43 vs 0.31 weighted) and drug abuse or dependence symptoms (0.47 vs 0.38) were larger than the weighted ones.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Estimated Effects of Early Alcohol Exposures on Adult Outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Table 2B
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusion that propensity-score estimates were biased by unmeasured confounding rests on a uniform attenuation that the table does not show for early intoxication, and the claim that early exposures predict adult alcohol problems within pairs holds only for early use, in all pairs, not in MZ pairs.

reporting_issues.issue: The exposure counts are given as 36% (505) and 15% (212) of the 'total sample', but the percentages correspond to the 1404 assessed at 14, not to the 1512 at intake (33% and 14%) (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Measures › Early Adolescent Alcohol Exposure Measures at Target Age 14
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; prevalence statements should name the FU1 sample as the denominator.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's Findings say that after propensity weighting several adult outcomes related to substance use or social functioning remained significantly associated with early alcohol exposure, but in Table 2A none of the outcomes the Results call social functioning or independence (family relationships, interpersonal problems, social engagement, adult independence) remained significant after weighting; besides the substance outcomes, the ones that did were antisocial symptoms and dependent stressful life events, which the Results describe separately.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Findings; Results › Estimated Effects of Early Alcohol Exposures on Adult Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 2A
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract should not be cited for effects on social functioning; the Results and the Discussion's last paragraph report no reliable effects on social functioning or independence.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion attributes the loss of significance for adult independence after weighting to confounding, but the coefficient hardly changed (early use 0.16, SE 0.07, unweighted against 0.15, SE 0.08, weighted; early intoxication 0.18 in both, SE 0.09 and 0.11): the weighting widened the standard error rather than removing the association. The unweighted association was with more independent adult functioning, not less.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Tables 2A and 2B, row 'Adult independence'
reporting_issues.consequence: The weighted data show this association estimated less precisely, not explained by confounding; within twin pairs the estimates were 0.00 and 0.01.
